content: Chorioamnionitis is a significant cause of perinatal morbidity and mortality. Amnioinfusion is a procedure designed to mitigate the adverse effects of chorioamnionitis by either diluting infectious organisms or exerting an antimicrobial effect through the infused fluid. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the impact of amnioinfusion on clinical and subclinical chorioamnionitis, fetal well-being, fetal heart rate patterns, and maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, as of July 6, 2016. The review focused on randomized clinical trials (RCTs) comparing amnioinfusion with no amnioinfusion in women diagnosed with chorioamnionitis. Trials involving sham amnioinfusion or different types or volumes of infusion fluid were also considered, but none were identified. Cluster-RCTs and quasi-RCTs were eligible for inclusion, but no such studies were found. One study published in abstract form was excluded due to the absence of numerical data. Cross-over study designs were deemed inappropriate and were not included. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and quality of the studies and extracted data, which were subsequently verified for accuracy. Only one small trial, involving 34 participants, met the inclusion criteria. This trial compared transcervical amnioinfusion with no amnioinfusion. The study was judged to have a high risk of bias due to its small sample size, inconsistent reporting, and lack of blinding information. Meta-analysis was not feasible due to the limited data. In the included trial, transcervical amnioinfusion was performed using room-temperature saline infused at a rate of 10 mL per minute for 60 minutes, followed by 3 mL per minute until delivery. All participants received an intrauterine pressure catheter, acetaminophen, and antibiotics (ampicillin or, for Group B beta streptococcal prophylaxis, penicillin and gentamycin). No trials using transabdominal amnioinfusion were identified. The trial found no clear effect of transcervical amnioinfusion on the incidence of postpartum endometritis (risk ratio [RR] 1.50, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.29 to 7.87; absolute risk 176/1000 versus 118/1000; low-quality evidence). Similarly, there was no clear effect on the incidence of neonatal infection (RR 3.00, 95% CI 0.13 to 68.84; absolute risk 0/1000 in both groups; low-quality evidence). The study did not report on perinatal death or severe morbidity, such as neonatal encephalopathy, intraventricular hemorrhage, or admission to intensive care. Regarding secondary outcomes, the rate of cesarean section was identical in both groups (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.35 to 2.83; absolute risk 294/1000 in both groups; low-quality evidence). There was no significant difference in the duration of maternal antibiotic treatment (mean difference [MD] 16 hours, 95% CI -1.75 to 33.75) or the duration of hospitalization (MD 3.00 hours, 95% CI -15.49 to 21.49). The study did not provide data on the number of neonates with a low Apgar score at five minutes. Women in the amnioinfusion group had a lower temperature at delivery compared to the control group (MD -0.38°C, 95% CI -0.74 to -0.02). However, this outcome was not pre-specified in the review protocol. Most secondary outcomes of interest were not reported in the included study. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of transcervical amnioinfusion for chorioamnionitis. The evidence does not support or refute the use of transcervical amnioinfusion outside of clinical trials. The single included study reported on a limited number of outcomes, and the small sample size precludes meaningful assessment of substantive outcomes. For outcomes assessed using the GRADE approach (postpartum endometritis, neonatal infection, and cesarean section), the quality of evidence was downgraded to low due to small sample size and lack of blinding information. The study did not report on the primary outcome of perinatal death or severe morbidity. The observed reduction in maternal temperature, though not a pre-specified outcome, may have implications for fetal well-being by reducing exposure to hyperthermia. This temperature reduction is hypothesized to result from the cooling effect of room-temperature fluid rather than a reduction in infection. Larger, well-designed randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm and expand upon these findings. Future research should include women with chorioamnionitis and compare transcervical or transabdominal amnioinfusion with no infusion. Outcomes should include maternal and perinatal measures, including neurodevelopmental assessments. Further investigation is warranted to explore the potential benefits and risks of amnioinfusion for chorioamnionitis and to assess the impact of temperature reduction on fetuses at risk of neurological damage.
